story: Just 17 days after Neptune was discovered in 1846, astronomer William Lassell spotted its massive moon, Triton. But Triton turned out to be a cosmic misfit. It is the only large moon in the Solar System that orbits backward, revolving in the exact opposite direction of its planet's rotation. Scientists believe Triton was once a dwarf planet in the icy Kuiper Belt before Neptune's gravity captured it. When NASA's Voyager 2 flew past in 1989, it revealed an active world plunged in deep freeze. With surface temperatures hovering around minus 235 degrees Celsius, Triton sports a bright ice shell that spews active nitrogen geysers eight kilometers into space. Beneath that frozen skin, scientists suspect a subsurface liquid ocean might exist. Yet Triton's backward orbit is slowly decaying, sealing its ultimate fate: billions of years from now, it will be pulled apart into a brilliant new ring around Neptune.
angle: Triton is the only large moon in the Solar System that orbits backward, spewing giant nitrogen geysers eight kilometers into space while spiraling toward its eventual destruction.
disputed: Exact timeframe until Triton reaches Neptune's Roche limit and breaks up: older studies estimated 3.6 billion years, while a 2025 study analyzed it to be 28 billion years. The script should attribute broadly by stating billions of years in the future.

Atmospheric pressure increase factor during summer: space.com mentions a fourfold increase since Voyager 2, while Wikipedia notes a pressure increase of up to a factor of three that later dropped back to Voyager levels by 2017. The script should mention summer atmospheric thickening generally without fixing a strict multiplication factor.
